cues.text: A Shepherd Turned Priest
Born in 1869 to a farming family in Totatiche, Jalisco, Cristóbal (Christopher) Magallanes tended his family's sheep as a boy before entering the seminary at nineteen.

Ordained a priest, he returned to serve his own home parish for over two decades, founding schools, a newspaper, catechetical centers, carpentry workshops, and agricultural cooperatives to serve his community's material as well as spiritual needs.
A Church Driven Underground

In the 1920s, the anti-clerical Mexican government under President Plutarco Elías Calles closed churches and seminaries, expelled foreign clergy, and made the public celebration of the sacraments a criminal offense.

When his own seminary was shut down, Cristóbal repeatedly reopened it in secret, moving from location to location and even continuing classes in private homes as authorities closed each successive attempt.
Falsely Accused

Cristóbal consistently wrote and preached against taking up arms, yet was falsely accused of supporting the Cristero rebellion — the armed Catholic uprising against the government's religious persecution.

Arrested in 1927 alongside a fellow priest, Fr. Agustín Caloca, he was executed without trial on May 25, 1927, his final words a declaration of innocence and forgiveness: "I am innocent and die innocent.
I forgive with all my heart those responsible for my death, and I ask God that my blood may serve to unite my Mexican brethren."
Twenty-Four Companions
Cristóbal's feast commemorates him together with twenty-four companions: twenty-one other diocesan priests and three laymen.

They were martyred not as a single group, but across more than twenty years and eight different Mexican states, during the broader persecution of the Catholic Church that gripped Mexico in the early twentieth century.
Viva Cristo Rey
These martyrs became particularly associated with the rallying cry of the Cristero movement, '¡Viva Cristo Rey!'
('Long live Christ the King').
Their deaths, whether by firing squad or hanging, were widely reported to have been met with calm forgiveness toward their executioners rather than bitterness or defiance.
Legacy
Canonized together by Pope John Paul II on May 21, 2000, Christopher Magallanes and his companions are remembered as emblematic witnesses.
They represent the Mexican Church's endurance through state persecution nearly unparalleled in the twentieth-century Americas.
Their patient, non-violent fidelity under threat of death stood alongside the more militant Cristero resistance as complementary responses to the same crisis of religious freedom.
